pos: n. (the edict of Frederick William of Brandenburg, 29 October 1685, inviting the French Protestants to his territories)
etymology: edict, from Latin edictum, a proclamation; Potsdam, the Brandenburg residence where it was signed.
biblical_def: The Edict of Potsdam was issued by Frederick William, the Great Elector of Brandenburg, on 29 October 1685, eleven days after Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes and made Protestant worship a crime in France. It is the most generous act of its kind in the century. The Elector offered the French Protestants free passage, with his agents at Amsterdam, Frankfurt and Hamburg to arrange it; land, houses and building materials; ten years' exemption from taxes and guild dues; admission to any trade without apprenticeship; their own churches with French-speaking ministers at the state's charge; and the same civil standing as his own subjects. Some twenty thousand came, with the weaving, hat-making, goldsmithing and market-gardening trades among them; within a generation one Berliner in five spoke French, and the French colony's church, schools and hospital were part of the city's fabric. A ruined, underpopulated electorate took in the refugees and was remade by them. “Let mine outcasts dwell with thee, Moab; be thou a covert to them from the face of the spoiler” (Isa 16:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an edict as a proclamation of command or prohibition by a sovereign, and a covert as a shelter, a defence.
webster_full: E'DICT, n. That which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order; a decree.
COV'ERT, n. A shelter; a defence; a hiding place; a thicket.
ELEC'TOR, n. A prince of the German Empire who had a voice in the election of the emperor.
OUT'CAST, n. One who is cast out or expelled; an exile; one driven from home or country.
scriptures: Isa 16:4
Let mine outcasts dwell with thee, Moab; be thou a covert to them from the face of the spoiler: for the extortioner is at an end, the spoiler ceaseth, the oppressors are consumed out of the land.
Isa 16:3
Take counsel, execute judgment; make thy shadow as the night in the midst of the noonday; hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth.
Thou shalt not deliver unto his master the servant which is escaped from his master unto thee:
If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain;
corruption_summary: Brandenburg's open door, eleven days after the Revocation.
corruption_paragraphs: The Edict of Potsdam is habitually explained away as pure calculation: a thinly populated state wanted skilled artisans and capital, and dressed self-interest as charity. The Elector did want them, and said so in the edict. He also stipulated French-language churches and ministers at his own cost, which no economic calculation required, and he admitted the poor and the aged with the weavers. Interest and mercy can run together, and the test is what a ruler does for those who bring him nothing.

The principle to recover is the standing law of refuge, which Israel was given in its plainest form — “Thou shalt not deliver unto his master the servant which is escaped from his master unto thee” (Deu 23:15) — and which Isaiah turns into a summons addressed even to Moab: “hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth” (Isa 16:3). The warning attached is against the sin of standing by: “If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death” (Pro 24:11).

“hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth” (Isa 16:3) — the law of refuge.
“If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death” (Pro 24:11) — the sin of the states that shut their ports.

pos: n. (the London district east of the City where Huguenot silk weavers settled after 1685)
etymology: From the fields of the medieval hospital of St Mary Spital; spital, a contraction of hospital.
biblical_def: Spitalfields lay just outside the City of London's eastern wall, and from the 1680s it became the densest Huguenot settlement in England. The refugees of the Revocation brought with them the silk-throwing and weaving trades of Tours and Lyons, and within two decades Spitalfields was producing brocades, damasks and figured silks that England had previously imported from France. The master weavers' houses still stand in Fournier Street and Wilkes Street with their long attic windows, built wide to light the loom. The district had its own French churches — La Patente in Brown's Lane, L'Église Neuve in Church Street, and others — its own schools and charities, and a French-speaking population of many thousands; by the end of the eighteenth century the congregations were English-speaking and the chapels passed to Methodists, Jews and later Muslims in turn. It is the clearest English case of persecution abroad enriching a trade at home. “Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings” (Pro 22:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a weaver as one whose occupation is to weave, and a loom as a frame in which a weaver works threads into cloth.
webster_full: WEA'VER, n. One whose occupation is to weave; one who works threads into cloth.
SILK, n. The fine soft thread produced by the silkworm; cloth made of silk.
LOOM, n. A frame or machine of wood or other material, in which a weaver works threads into cloth.
DIL'IGENT, a. Steady in application to business; constant in effort; assiduous.
scriptures: Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.

Them hath he filled with wisdom of heart, to work all manner of work, of the engraver, and of the cunning workman, and of the embroiderer, in blue, and in purple, in scarlet, and in fine linen, and of the weaver, even of them that do any work, and of those that devise cunning work.
Exo 31:3
And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship,
For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
corruption_summary: French silk looms in London attics, and the chapels that followed them.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the sentimentality of the heritage trade, which has made Spitalfields a set of handsome Georgian frontages with a Huguenot label and little else. The men who built those houses came because dragoons were billeted in their homes until they recanted, and the long attic windows are there because a weaver who had lost everything had to work by daylight.

The principle to recover is that skilled handwork is a gift of God's Spirit and named as such in Scripture, not a lesser calling beneath the learned ones. The craftsmen of the tabernacle are described in terms no modern account of labour improves on: “Them hath he filled with wisdom of heart, to work all manner of work, of the engraver, and of the cunning workman, and of the embroiderer” (Exo 35:35). Bezaleel's qualification is stated as an endowment: “And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship” (Exo 31:3).

pos: n. pl. (the Walloon and Huguenot weaving congregation at Canterbury, worshipping in the cathedral crypt from 1575)
etymology: Canterbury, Old English Cantwaraburh, the stronghold of the men of Kent; weaver, from Old English wefan, to weave.
biblical_def: The Canterbury weavers were Walloon Protestants who came over from the southern Netherlands in the 1560s, fleeing Alva's repression, and were licensed by the city and by Archbishop Parker to settle, work and worship. From 1575 they were granted the use of the undercroft of Canterbury Cathedral — the Norman crypt beneath the choir — for their services in French, and they have worshipped there ever since, the oldest continuous French-speaking congregation in England. They brought the broadcloth and silk trades that made Canterbury a weaving town for two centuries; at their height they were perhaps two thousand people in a city of five thousand, with their own looms, discipline and poor-relief. The Huguenots of the Revocation reinforced them a century later. The arrangement is a remarkable thing to picture: a Reformed congregation of foreign refugees singing metrical psalms in French directly under the choir of the English primate's own cathedral. “Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself” (Psa 84:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a crypt as a subterranean cell or chapel, and broadcloth as a woollen cloth of fine texture and broad width.
webster_full: CRYPT, n. A subterranean cell or cave, especially under a church, for the interment of persons.
BROAD'CLOTH, n. A species of woollen cloth of a fine texture and a broad width.
UN'DERCROFT, n. A vault under a building; a subterranean apartment.
ASY'LUM, n. A sanctuary or place of refuge, where criminals and debtors found shelter.
scriptures: Psa 84:3
Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O LORD of hosts, my King, and my God.
Heb 13:3
Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:
And on the sabbath we went out of the city by a river side, where prayer was wont to be made; and we sat down, and spake unto the women which resorted thither.
corruption_summary: A French Reformed congregation in the crypt of Canterbury Cathedral since 1575.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a confessional embarrassment handled by silence: the crypt congregation is an awkward fact for accounts of the Elizabethan church as uniformly episcopal in its sympathies, since here a Reformed congregation with its own elders, discipline and French psalmody was licensed by an archbishop and housed in his own cathedral. It is usually mentioned as a curiosity rather than as evidence.

The principle to recover is that receiving the persecuted is a duty measured by identification rather than by charity at a distance: “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body” (Heb 13:3). The Lord puts the same thing in the first person at the judgment: “I was a stranger, and ye took me in” (Mat 25:35).

“Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3) — the duty Canterbury discharged.

pos: n. (the Huguenot settlement on the James River in Virginia, founded 1700)
etymology: From Monacan, the Siouan people whose abandoned village stood on the site; anglicised as Manakin.
biblical_def: Manakin Town was the chief Huguenot settlement in Virginia, planted in 1700 and 1701 some twenty miles above the falls of the James River, on the site of a deserted Monacan village. Between six and seven hundred refugees came in four shiploads, sent from England where they had gathered after the Revocation, with William III's encouragement and a grant of ten thousand acres; the Virginia Assembly exempted them from taxes for seven years and set them up as King William Parish, a French-speaking parish within the established church of the colony. The first years were very hard: the land was poor for wheat, the mortality was heavy, and the settlers petitioned repeatedly for relief. They turned to tobacco and to vine-growing, intermarried with their English neighbours, and within two generations the parish was English-speaking and the names — Maury, Flournoy, Dupuy, Michaux, Trabue — had become Virginian. “By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country” (Heb 11:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to sojourn as to dwell for a time, and a plantation as a colony or the place where a colony is settled.
webster_full: PLANTA'TION, n. The place planted; a colony; an original settlement in a new country.
SO'JOURN, v. To dwell for a time; to live in a place as a temporary resident or as a stranger.
PAR'ISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the people under his care.
WIL'DERNESS, n. A desert; a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited.
scriptures: Heb 11:9
By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise:
Gen 12:1
Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:
They wandered in the wilderness in a solitary way; they found no city to dwell in.
And he led them forth by the right way, that they might go to a city of habitation.
corruption_summary: Seven hundred Huguenots on the James River, English-speaking within two generations.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the genealogical romance that has grown around Manakin Town, in which the settlement is remembered chiefly as the origin of distinguished Virginian families and the first decade's destitution drops out. The parish records and the petitions to the Assembly are plain about what it cost; a good many of those who landed did not survive the second winter.

The principle to recover is that the patriarchal life of faith was a life without a settled title, and that Scripture treats this as the normal shape of the pilgrim's condition rather than as a misfortune: “By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles” (Heb 11:9). The psalm of the redeemed begins exactly where Manakin Town began — “They wandered in the wilderness in a solitary way; they found no city to dwell in” (Psa 107:4) — and does not stay there: “And he led them forth by the right way, that they might go to a city of habitation” (Psa 107:7).

“Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred” (Gen 12:1) — four shiploads out of France by way of England.

pos: n. (the Huguenot settlement in Westchester, New York, founded 1688)
etymology: Named for La Rochelle, the Atlantic port that was the Huguenot stronghold besieged in 1627–28; Rochelle, the little rock.
biblical_def: New Rochelle was founded in 1688 on the Sound in Westchester County, New York, by about thirty Huguenot families who had left France after the Revocation, come by way of England, and bought some six thousand acres from John Pell, lord of the manor of Pelham. They named it for La Rochelle, the Atlantic fortress-port from which many of them came and which Richelieu had broken sixty years before. They walked the twenty-three miles to the French church in New York City for the Lord's Supper until they could build their own, farmed, fished and traded, and sent their children to a French school that drew pupils from New York; Jacob Leisler, the New York Huguenot leader, had helped arrange the purchase. The congregation became Anglican in the eighteenth century and English-speaking soon after, as all these settlements did. The name is now a suburb and keeps a memory most of its residents could not explain. “And there he maketh the hungry to dwell, that they may prepare a city for habitation” (Psa 107:36).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a settlement as the act of settling or a colony newly established, and a manor as the land belonging to a lord.
webster_full: SET'TLEMENT, n. The act of settling; establishment in life or in a place; a colony newly established.
MAN'OR, n. The land belonging to a lord or nobleman, held by him in his own hand.
REFUGEE', n. One who flies to a shelter or place of safety; one who flees to a foreign country.
HAB'ITATION, n. Place of abode; a settled dwelling; a mansion; a residence.
scriptures: And there he maketh the hungry to dwell, that they may prepare a city for habitation;

And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
Deu 8:7
For the LORD thy God bringeth thee into a good land, a land of brooks of water, of fountains and depths that spring out of valleys and hills;
corruption_summary: Thirty Huguenot families in Westchester, named for the fortress they lost.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a general one about the whole Huguenot diaspora in America: these settlements are now remembered as ethnic footnotes, and the thing that produced them — a state deciding that a confession of faith was a crime — is treated as remote and impossible. It was legislated in the most advanced country in Europe within living memory of men who founded New Rochelle.

The principle to recover is that God appoints where the nations live and that no displacement falls outside his determination: “And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26). Isaiah's word to a people rebuilding names their calling in the very work: “thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in” (Isa 58:12).

pos: n. (Jacques Abbadie, 1654–1727, Huguenot pastor at Berlin and London, Dean of Killaloe, apologist)
etymology: French Jacques, from Hebrew Yaaqob through Latin Jacobus; Abbadie, a Béarnais name from Occitan abadia, an abbey.
biblical_def: Jacques Abbadie was born at Nay in Béarn, educated at Puylaurens, Saumur and Sedan, and at twenty-six was invited by the Great Elector to be pastor of the French church in Berlin, where he served the growing refugee colony for eight years. He followed Marshal Schomberg to England and then to Ireland, preached at the Savoy in London to the French congregation there, was given the deanery of Killaloe, and spent his last years in Marylebone. His reputation rests on the Traité de la vérité de la religion chrétienne of 1684, which went through many editions and translations and was among the most widely read defences of the Christian faith of its century; he followed it with a treatise on the deity of Christ and one on the knowledge of oneself. He preached and wrote for a people whose faith was being attacked on both sides at once, by a Catholic state that had outlawed them and by the rising deism of the salons, and the ground he always came back to was the resurrection. “whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead” (Act 17:31).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an apologist as one who defends by argument, and assurance as full confidence, certain expectation, ground of certainty.
webster_full: APOL'OGIST, n. One who makes an apology; one who defends or excuses by argument.
ASSU'RANCE, n. Certain expectation; full confidence; firm persuasion; ground of certainty.
DE'ISM, n. The doctrine or creed of a deist; the belief or system of those who deny revelation.
DEAN, n. A dignitary of the church; the second dignitary of a diocese.
scriptures: Because he hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he hath ordained; whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead.
Act 1:3
To whom also he shewed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs, being seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God:
For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
Luk 1:4
That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.
corruption_summary: The Béarnais pastor whose defence of the faith outsold the deists who attacked it.
corruption_paragraphs: Abbadie wrote against the earliest form of a claim that has governed educated unbelief ever since: that the Christian religion is a worthy moral system whose historical and miraculous claims may be quietly set aside. His answer was that the faith is a report of events and stands or falls with them, and that a Christianity reduced to its ethics has no authority to impose even the ethics. Three centuries of attempts to keep the morality and drop the resurrection have not improved on the objection.

The principle to recover is that God has staked the judgment of the world on an event in history and offered that event as the evidence: “whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead” (Act 17:31). Luke speaks of “many infallible proofs” (Act 1:3), and Peter rules out the alternative reading in advance: “For we have not followed cunningly devised fables” (2Pe 1:16).

pos: n. (Pierre du Bosc, 1623–1692, pastor of Caen, the foremost Huguenot preacher of his generation)
etymology: French Pierre, from Greek petros, a stone; du Bosc, of the wood, a Norman form of bois.
biblical_def: Pierre du Bosc was pastor of the Reformed church at Caen for thirty-eight years and was reckoned by friends and enemies the greatest French preacher of his time. In 1668 the churches of France chose him to carry their complaint to the court over the suppression of their chambers and colleges, and he spoke before Louis XIV in a private audience; the king is reported to have said afterwards that he had never heard a man speak better. It changed nothing. The pressure increased year by year, du Bosc was exiled from Caen in 1685 and the Revocation followed within months; he went to Rotterdam, where he preached to the Walloon church for his last seven years and where his sermons were printed. He is the pattern of the eloquent man who is heard, admired, and refused: a reminder that the finest preaching cannot compel, and that the answer to it is as likely to be a compliment as a conversion. “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver” (Pro 25:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eloquence as the art of speaking with fluency and power to persuade, and an audience as a hearing granted by a prince.
webster_full: EL'OQUENCE, n. The art of expressing thought with fluency, force and elegance; oratory.
AU'DIENCE, n. A hearing; admittance to a hearing; a formal interview granted by a prince.
PREACH'ER, n. One who discourses publicly on religious subjects.
FIT'LY, adv. Suitably; properly; with propriety; in a manner adapted to the purpose.
scriptures: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
The preacher sought to find out acceptable words: and that which was written was upright, even words of truth.
The heart of the wise teacheth his mouth, and addeth learning to his lips.
But when they deliver you up, take no thought how or what ye shall speak: for it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak.
corruption_summary: The preacher Louis XIV admired and did not heed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a persistent evangelical overestimate of eloquence — the assumption that a hearing well won is a cause half gained, and that if only the case were put ably enough the hearer must yield. Du Bosc put it as ably as it has ever been put, to the most powerful man in Europe, who praised the performance and signed the Revocation seventeen years later.

The principle to recover is that fit speech is a real gift to be sought and prepared for, and that its effect is not in the speaker's hands. Solomon commends the craft without qualification — “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver” (Pro 25:11) — and the Preacher describes the labour of finding such words: “The preacher sought to find out acceptable words” (Ecc 12:10). The Lord's promise to men summoned before rulers rests the matter elsewhere entirely: “it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak” (Mat 10:19).

pos: n. (David Ancillon, 1617–1692, pastor of Metz for forty years, then of the French colony at Berlin)
etymology: Hebrew David, beloved; Ancillon, a French family name of the Metz region.
biblical_def: David Ancillon was pastor of the Reformed church of Metz from 1653, for more than thirty years, in a city where Protestants and Catholics lived under close supervision and where his learning and temper made him respected across the divide. At the Revocation in 1685 the Metz congregation was broken up and he was given a fortnight to leave France; he went first to Frankfurt and then to Berlin, where the Great Elector, under the Edict of Potsdam, made him pastor and judge of the French colony. He died there in 1692. The Ancillon family is the clearest single instance of what the Refuge did for Brandenburg: his son Charles was the royal historiographer and director of the French colony; later Ancillons were pastors, jurists and, in the next century, a Prussian foreign minister. A man expelled with a fortnight's notice founded a line that served the state that took him in. “If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning” (Psa 137:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colony as a body of people transplanted from their mother country, and exile as banishment from one's country.

HISTORIOG'RAPHER, n. A historian; a writer of history, especially one appointed by authority.

scriptures: If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning.
If I do not remember thee, let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth; if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy.
And truly, if they had been mindful of that country from whence they came out, they might have had opportunity to have returned.
But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.
corruption_summary: Expelled from Metz with a fortnight's notice, pastor of Berlin's French colony.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the comfortable reading of the Refuge as a success story — talented people found better opportunities elsewhere and everybody gained. Ancillon was sixty-eight years old with a fortnight to leave the city where he had ministered for thirty-two years, and the congregation he left behind was not transplanted but dissolved. What was gained in Berlin was not what was lost in Metz.

The principle to recover is that the exile's love for the place he has lost is right, and that it is not to be cured but subordinated. The psalmist makes forgetting Jerusalem a self-curse — “let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth; if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy” (Psa 137:6) — and Hebrews shows the patriarchs refusing the opportunity to return because their eye was on a better country: “But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Heb 11:16).

pos: n. (Elie Benoist, 1640–1728, pastor of Alençon, historian of the Edict of Nantes)
etymology: Hebrew Eliyahu, the LORD is God, through French Élie; Benoist, the French form of Benedictus, blessed.
biblical_def: Elie Benoist was pastor at Alençon in Normandy until the Revocation drove him out in 1685, and he spent the remaining forty-three years of his life at Delft, pastor of the Walloon church there. His monument is the Histoire de l'Édit de Nantes, published at Delft in five quarto volumes between 1693 and 1695: a documentary history of the French Reformed churches from the Edict of 1598 to its revocation, built out of the edicts, declarations, judgments, synodal acts and local records that he and his correspondents could gather. He wrote it while the events were within living memory and while the documents still existed, many of which were later destroyed, and it remains a primary source for the whole period that no later historian can bypass. He understood what he was doing: the churches had been abolished by law and their very existence was being written out of the record, and a history with the documents printed in it could not be unsaid. “This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a document as a written instrument conveying information or proof, and a record as a register, an authentic account of facts.
webster_full: DOC'UMENT, n. A written instrument conveying information; anything serving as proof or evidence.
REC'ORD, n. A register; an authentic or official copy of any writing; a memorial.
HIS'TORY, n. An account of facts, particularly of facts respecting nations or states, in the order of time.
GENERA'TION, n. A single succession of living beings in natural descent; the people of the same period.
scriptures: This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
Psa 56:8
Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?
Job 8:8
For enquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers:
corruption_summary: The exiled pastor who wrote the documentary history of the churches France abolished.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a methodological fashion that would discount Benoist because he was a party to what he described: the victim, it is said, cannot be the historian. The objection is worth less than it sounds. Benoist printed the documents, including the crown's own edicts and declarations, and invited his readers to weigh them; a history that prints its evidence is more easily checked than one that summarises it.

The principle to recover is that the church is commanded to keep and hand on the record of God's dealings with it, including the record of its sufferings: “We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4). The psalmist's confidence is that nothing is lost in the keeping: “Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?” (Psa 56:8).

“We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4) — a history written from the documents.
“Thou tellest my wanderings” (Psa 56:8) — the churches France legislated out of existence.

pos: n. (Jacques Saurin, 1677–1730, pastor of the Walloon church at The Hague, the greatest preacher of the Refuge)
etymology: French Jacques, from Hebrew Yaaqob through Latin Jacobus; Saurin, a Provençal family name.
biblical_def: Jacques Saurin was eight years old at Nîmes when the Revocation came, and his father took the family to Geneva. He served briefly as a soldier in Piedmont, then studied at Geneva, ministered to the French congregation in London for five years, and in 1705 was called to the Walloon church at The Hague, where he preached for twenty-five years to a congregation of refugees, diplomats and princes, and became the most celebrated pulpit orator in the Protestant world. His sermons were printed in his lifetime and reprinted for two centuries, in French, Dutch, German and English; they are long, closely argued, and relentless in application, and they are directed above all at the hearer who agrees with everything and does nothing. He was attacked late in life over a treatise on whether a lie may ever be justified, and the controversy embittered his last years. He died at The Hague in 1730. “Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men” (2Co 5:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to persuade as to influence by argument or expostulation, and application as the act of applying a doctrine to a hearer.
webster_full: PERSUADE', v. To influence by argument, advice or expostulation; to draw or incline the will.
APPLICA'TION, n. The act of applying; the employment of means; in preaching, the practical use of doctrine.
OR'ATOR, n. A public speaker; one who pronounces a discourse publicly.
TER'ROR, n. Extreme fear; violent dread; the cause of extreme fear.
scriptures: Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men; but we are made manifest unto God; and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences.
Act 2:37
Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do?
Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
Isa 58:1
Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins.
corruption_summary: The Hague pulpit that preached to men who agreed with everything and did nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: Saurin's great subject is the thing he called the condition of the half-Christian: the hearer who assents to every doctrine, attends every service, could defend the faith in argument, and whose life is untouched. He pursued it because his congregation was full of such men — refugees in the second generation, prosperous now, holding a confession their fathers had suffered for and feeling nothing. The condition is not period-bound, and it is the besetting disease of every settled and orthodox church.

The principle to recover is that preaching aims at the will and not only at the understanding, and that the word is given a power to divide a man from himself: “the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit” (Heb 4:12). Pentecost shows what it is for when it is working: “Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart” (Act 2:37).
